side_a_arguments: Community engagement around Northgate Mall produced confusion and failed to reflect neighborhood priorities compared to Braggtown outreach.
Delaying UDO adoption slows implementation of Comprehensive Plan housing and equitable growth policies.
conflicts.side_b_position: Preserve thorough Planning Commission deliberation across multiple meetings rather than rushing the UDO rewrite.
side_b_arguments: Planning Commissioners cannot responsibly digest a massive new development code and zoning map in a single rushed session.
North Carolina state restrictions on downzoning make getting the initial UDO mapping right even more consequential.

meetings.title: Special City Council Meeting Nov. 16, 2026 at 5PM
meetings.presiding_chair: Mayor Pro Tem Patempo Lieto (Mayor running late; called to order by Mayor Pro Tem)
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council held a special meeting on November 16, 2026, featuring a comprehensive presentation and discussion on the upcoming City Compensation Classification Study led by Gallagher consultants and HR Chief Erin Miley. The council reviewed market benchmarking methodologies, pay structure designs (step vs. open range), and strategies for mitigating wage compression. A significant portion of the meeting was devoted to a robust debate regarding the Durham Minimum Livable Wage (DMLW), its rent-based formula, projected increases exceeding $27/hour, and the resulting compression on lower-tier step plans, leading to a directive for staff to return with options and draft ordinance language.

agenda_items.title: Presentation on Compensation Classification Study and Durham Minimum Livable Wage (DMLW) Framework
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Erin Miley (Chief HR Officer) and Gallagher consultants Jamie Parker and Susie Parker presented the framework, methodology, and timeline for the City of Durham's upcoming Compensation Classification Study. The study aims to evaluate all job classifications, benchmark against comparator markets, address wage compression, and review compensation philosophy. Council members engaged in extensive discussion regarding timeline, compression challenges, and specifically the Durham Minimum Livable Wage (DMLW), which is projected to rise significantly under its current rent-based formula.
agenda_items.vote_summary: No formal vote was taken; council provided feedback and directed staff/city attorney to bring back options and draft ordinance/resolution language regarding DMLW adjustments and methodology for future budget cycles.

disagreements.meeting_title: Special City Council Meeting Nov. 16, 2026 at 5PM
disagreements.issue: Whether and how to adjust, pause, or reform the Durham Minimum Livable Wage (DMLW) calculation and implementation for the upcoming fiscal year to prevent severe wage compression.
disagreements.summary: Debate centered on balancing the progressive goals of the Durham Minimum Livable Wage with the severe wage compression and structural distortions it causes when out-pacing the rest of the compensation plan.
disagreements.side_a_position: Support a temporary pause/holding of DMLW at current levels while studying alternative methodologies to protect the pay plan from severe compression.
side_a_arguments: City Manager and HR administration argued that strictly following the current DMLW formula would push the wage above $27/hr, severely compressing the lower half of step plans and harming long-tenured employees unless massive additional funds are committed. Recommended exploring alternative calculation methodologies and holding the DMLW at the previous year's rate for one year as a pause/interim measure.
side_a_members: Manager Wanda Page (referenced/implied), Erin Miley, Mayor Pro Tem Patempo Lieto
disagreements.side_b_position: Cautious of pausing or lowering DMLW standards without careful study; preferred exploring structural alternatives without dismantling ordinance protections.
side_b_arguments: Several council members expressed strong attachment to the DMLW ordinance as a vital anti-poverty asset, voiced reluctance to 'chip away' or 'pause' it, and noted concerns about worker morale and trust, while acknowledging the severe budget and compression realities.
side_b_members: Council Member Rist, Council Member Cook, Council Member Burris
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote taken; council directed the City Attorney and administration to return with draft language and options (such as interim rates or alternative methodologies) for council review prior to budget deliberations.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham Joint City County Planning Committee (JCCPC) - November 4, 2026
disagreements.issue: Data Center UDO Regulations: Square-Footage Caps, Separation Buffers, Review Process, and RTP/Medical Exemptions
disagreements.summary: Committee members split over how restrictive Durham's permanent post-moratorium data center ordinance should be regarding maximum building size, residential/institutional buffers, legislative rezoning requirements, and exemptions for Research Triangle Park (RTP) and medical infrastructure.
disagreements.side_a_position: Favor stricter urban size limits, clear legislative oversight, environmental/air-quality transparency, and tailored exemptions for critical medical systems.
side_a_arguments: Nate Baker questioned whether a 100,000-square-foot cap is far too large inside urban city limits compared to RTP/county sites, suggesting 10,000-25,000 sq ft in the city and preventing 10% expansion loopholes above the cap.
Matt Kopac requested exploring municipal electric authority and state legislative advocacy on air-quality/generator emissions while confirming legal limits on development-plan proffers.

Javiera Caballero emphasized non-discriminatory institutional protections so hospital/clinical systems (such as Duke MyChart servers) and small embedded data facilities are not ensnared in lengthy rezoning processes.
disagreements.side_b_position: Protect RTP and Treyburn economic competitiveness from excessive buffers or multi-year approval delays.
side_b_arguments: County Commissioner Wendy Jacobs and County colleagues stressed that RTP already hosts 14 data centers and recently absorbed roughly 6,000 federal-impact job losses, making Treyburn and RTP tech investment economically vital.
County members warned that 2,000-foot separation buffers would effectively lock out many existing RTP industrial parcels and objected to overly protracted review timelines.
disagreements.resolution: No formal vote taken; staff committed to returning in December with refined draft UDO text options and cost/comparative benchmarks for committee review ahead of the January 2027 Planning Commission hearing.

votes.item_title: Local Historic Landmark Designation for Cranford-Wanamaker House (1019 West Trinity Ave)
votes.notes: Passed unanimously after public hearing and presentation.
votes.discussion_detail: The Durham City Council considered a local historic landmark designation for the Cranford-Wanamaker House located at 1019 West Trinity Avenue. Public comments touched upon historic preservation merits, review processes, and potential tax revenue implications. Staff addressed council inquiries regarding why this landmark designation is the most fitting protection mechanism compared to other preservation options. Following discussion, the motion passed unanimously with no recorded opposition.

votes.item_title: Voluntary Annexation and Utility Extension Agreement for 508 Olive Branch Road (JC Construction LLC)
votes.notes: Passed 6-1 with Councilmember Baker voting no.
votes.discussion_detail: The City Council considered a voluntary annexation, utility extension agreement, and initial zoning map change for 0.462 acres located at 508 Olive Branch Road requested by Stuart Proctor LLC (JC Construction LLC) to connect a single-family home to water and sewer. Council member Baker raised questions regarding how Underbrush Drive terminates at the property and whether a through-connection or cul-de-sac was contemplated by prior development, with staff noting that transportation rules under the UDO do not require connecting the roads. Other council members supported the annexation, emphasizing the environmental benefits of connecting homes to municipal water and sewer to mitigate failing septic tanks and reduce phosphorus and nitrogen runoff into local lakes. The motion passed 6-1, with Council member Baker voting in opposition.

votes.item_title: UDO Zoning Map Change for 508 Olive Branch Road (Watershed Protection Overlay City Jurisdiction)
votes.notes: Passed unanimously.
votes.discussion_detail: The Council considered a UDO zoning map change to remove 508 Olive Branch Road from the county jurisdiction of the residential rural Falls Jordan District B watershed protection overlay and establish the same under city jurisdiction. Following the discussion on the associated annexation and utility extension, the motion was duly moved, seconded, and passed unanimously.

votes.item_title: Consistency Statement for 508 Olive Branch Road per NCGS 160D-605
votes.notes: Passed unanimously.
votes.discussion_detail: The Council considered the required consistency statement for the 508 Olive Branch Road annexation and zoning map change pursuant to North Carolina General Statute Section 160D-605. The statutory consistency statement was moved, seconded, and adopted by a unanimous vote.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session October 8, 2026 (partial)
disagreements.issue: Homeless Encampment Accountability Resolution and Timing Ahead of Full Council Return
disagreements.summary: Council divided sharply over whether to advance Council Member Nate Baker's draft resolution establishing formal notice, shelter-offer, and property-storage requirements for homeless encampment clearings immediately or defer policy design to City staff and a full 7-member Council committee after December.
disagreements.side_a_position: Advance immediate interim encampment accountability guardrails through a Council resolution before potential state HB 437 veto override.
side_a_arguments: Nate Baker argued Durham lacks enforceable written protocols requiring adequate notice, appropriate shelter alternatives, property storage, and complaint review before clearing encampments.
Chelsea Cook backed moving promptly on basic accountability standards for unsheltered residents rather than waiting months for broader committee processes.
disagreements.side_b_position: Avoid rushing an unvetted resolution without City Manager feasibility feedback, recognize neighborhood public-safety enforcement near schools, and wait until the full Council returns in December.
side_b_arguments: Shanetta Burris strongly pushed back against framing Operation Safe Passage or city crews' actions near Fayetteville and Pilot Streets as targeting homeless residents rather than addressing open-air drug trafficking, overdoses, and threats near schools, asking 'do you want to be right or do you want to win?'
Matt Kopac and Javiera Caballero favored a staff-informed policy process or mayor-appointed subcommittee once all seven seated council members are back in December (Dec 10).

meetings.title: Durham Joint City County Planning Committee (JCCPC) - October 7, 2026
meetings.executive_summary: At the October 7, 2026 JCCPC meeting chaired by Nate Baker, the committee approved the September 2 minutes and focused on three major planning initiatives. Staff presented recommendations to tighten green-building rezoning commitments under Comprehensive Plan Policies 49, 96, and 108 by tying certifications to pre-Certificate of Occupancy (COC) verification and dropping Energy Star and Green Globes, prompting debate between affordability/small-builder cost concerns raised by Javiera Caballero and stronger sustainability mandates backed by Matt Kopac and Wendy Jacobs. Growth Management staff then delivered the FY24-26 Growth Management Trends and Analysis Report—documenting 107 private cases, 2,746 proffered affordable units, and mixed-use land losses—followed by an update from Planning and Three Oaks Engineering pivoting the Multimodal Development Standards (MMDS) toward a site-plan point-based system.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, Agenda Adjustment, and Approval of September 2 Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Nate Baker called roll with Javiera Caballero, Matt Kopac, Planning Commission Chair Chagaris, and County Commissioner Wendy Jacobs present, achieving quorum when Commissioner Stephen Valentine arrived shortly thereafter. The committee reordered the agenda to hear Item 6 ahead of Item 5 and unanimously approved the September 2, 2026 minutes.

agenda_items.title: Green Building Commitments and Comprehensive Plan Policies 49, 96, and 108
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff (Brianna Bettle, Payton Burgess, and Bo Dobrzenski) recommended updating rezoning proffer guidance to require pre-COC verification, drop Energy Star and Green Globes, exclude Greenguard as a standalone building certification, add Enterprise Green Communities for urban heat island mitigation (Policy 96), and specify green stormwater infrastructure (Policy 108). Javiera Caballero cautioned against pricing out small and local builders without cost data, tiers, or LIHTC subsidies, whereas Matt Kopac and Wendy Jacobs pressed for strong energy-efficiency standards and LDC sustainability matrix alignment.

agenda_items.title: Growth Management Trends and Analysis Report (Oct 2023 - June 2026)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Andy Lester, Sarah Vinas, Aaron Cain, and Scott Whiteman reported trends across 107 private cases since the 2023 Comprehensive Plan adoption: 92 City approvals (76 consistent, 16 inconsistent) and 12 denials, 223 net acres added to residential while losing 112 Mixed Neighborhood and 42 TOA acres, ~5,000 housing units built annually, and 2,746 active proffered affordable units tracked with Housing and Neighborhood Services. Members requested adding EMS/County revenue to Fiscal Impact Analysis, creating a one-page public rezoning packet summary, and visualizing annual growth metrics.

agenda_items.title: Multimodal Development Standards (MMDS) Point-Based Update
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Lisa Miller and Three Oaks Engineering consultant Jennifer Baldwin presented a revised approach shifting Multimodal TIA away from a vehicular model toward a four-category site-plan point system (pedestrian, bicycle, transit, and street design) calibrated by acreage (<2 or >2 acres), place type, and Tier 1/2 context questions. Chair Baker and Mayor Pro Tem Caballero described themselves as open-minded skeptics, questioning whether point-trading could erode essential safety standards like tight curb radii and urging test-runs on past cases, while Kopac warned against excessive administrative complexity.

agenda_items.title: Community Planning Program Projects
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The monthly Community Planning Program tracker was included on the agenda as informational material only with no staff presentation or committee questions before adjournment at 12:37 p.m.

votes.item_title: Approval of September 2, 2026 JCCPC Minutes
votes.notes: Joint City-County Planning Committee voice vote; Planning Commission Chair Chagaris and County Commissioners Wendy Jacobs and Stephen Valentine were also present after Valentine's arrival established quorum.
votes.discussion_detail: After County Commissioner Stephen Valentine arrived to establish a JCCPC quorum and the committee agreed to move Item 6 ahead of Item 5 on the agenda, Chair Nate Baker called for action on the September 2, 2026 meeting minutes. No committee members offered corrections or amendments to the record. A member moved to approve the minutes and a second followed without debate. All present members voted 'Aye' unanimously on a voice vote.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham Joint City County Planning Committee (JCCPC) - October 7, 2026
disagreements.issue: Cost and Accessibility Impacts of Tightened Green Building Rezoning Standards (Policies 49, 96, 108)
disagreements.summary: Committee members differed on how aggressively to tighten third-party green building certifications and pre-COC enforcement mechanisms in rezoning proffers without disadvantaging smaller local builders or affordable housing projects.
disagreements.side_a_position: Warn against overly rigid certification mandates without cost transparency, tiered options, contractor training, and affordable-housing financial support.
side_a_arguments: Javiera Caballero urged colleagues 'don't let perfect be the enemy of good,' warning that eliminating accessible options without cost breakdowns could price out smaller homegrown builders.
Caballero called for tiered scoring options, contractor workshops, and clarity on whether City subsidies cover compliance costs on LIHTC and affordable housing developments.
disagreements.side_b_position: Eliminate weak or unenforceable building-certification checkboxes in favor of rigorous pre-COC verified standards and utility-lowering sustainability commitments.
side_b_arguments: Matt Kopac and County Commissioner Wendy Jacobs stressed that strong energy-efficiency standards directly lower household utility burdens and advance County green-building goals.

Staff and proponents noted Energy Star and Green Globes posed timing and enforcement problems prior to Certificate of Occupancy and advocated stronger integration with the draft LDC sustainability matrix.
disagreements.resolution: Informational guidance provided to staff; no formal vote taken, with staff noting how LDC matrix standards would differentiate baseline rules from discretionary rezoning proffers.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham Joint City County Planning Committee (JCCPC) - October 7, 2026
disagreements.issue: Multimodal Development Standards (MMDS): Flexibility vs. Predictability and Non-Negotiable Safety Standards
disagreements.summary: Members questioned whether Three Oaks Engineering's proposed site-plan point-based Multimodal Development Standards would create loopholes around core street-safety features or add unnecessary complexity.
disagreements.side_a_position: Express skepticism about point-trading menus and require real-case stress testing before endorsing the framework.
side_a_arguments: Nate Baker warned that an elective point system could let developers trade away foundational safety features such as tight intersection curb radii for less impactful amenities.
Javiera Caballero requested testing the proposed point matrix on a past real development case to confirm predictable outcomes for both applicants and neighbors.
Matt Kopac cautioned against introducing excessive technical complexity into site-plan review.
disagreements.side_b_position: Support replacing car-centric level-of-service models with a context-sensitive multimodal point system usable across urban and suburban sites.
side_b_arguments: Staff and Three Oaks Engineering argued a two-tier, acreage- and place-type-calibrated point framework avoids rigid one-size-fits-all mandates and exempts small projects while aligning with eventual LDC adoption.
disagreements.resolution: Informational feedback collected for Three Oaks Engineering and Planning staff to refine and test the draft methodology.

meetings.title: Durham City Council October 5, 2026
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council held its regular meeting on October 5, 2026, opening with ceremonial proclamations for National Disability Employment Awareness Month, Children's Health Equity Month, Energy Efficiency Day, and Hispanic Latino Heritage Month. The main legislative item discussed and voted upon was a zoning and annexation request for 3815 Wake Forest Highway, which sparked a robust debate regarding housing density, environmental impacts, infrastructure, and developer proffers. The council ultimately voted 4-3 to approve the annexation and utility extension, 4-3 to approve the UDO zoning amendment, and unanimously to adopt the consistency statement.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, and Pledge of Allegiance
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams called the Durham City Council regular meeting to order with a moment of silence. Council Member Wrist led the Pledge of Allegiance. Madam Clerk called the roll, confirming all council members present.

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Proclamations and Performances
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The council presented several proclamations recognizing National Disability Employment Awareness Month, Children's Health Equity Month (Harper's Home), Energy Efficiency Day (Ashrae), and Hispanic Heritage Month, accompanied by community remarks and cultural performances.

agenda_items.title: Council Member Reports and Comments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council members shared community updates, congratulated local events like Durham Pride and NCCU Homecoming, discussed intercity visits, and raised concerns regarding local violent crime, infrastructure, and housing affordability.

agenda_items.title: State and Federal Lobbying Services Contracts
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The council debated and voted on contracts for state and federal lobbying services, discussing the cost, effectiveness, and strategic necessity of retaining lobbying representation in Raleigh and Washington D.C.
agenda_items.vote_summary: State lobbying contract passed 4-3; Federal lobbying contract passed unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing & Action: 3815 Wake Forest Highway Annexation and UDO Zoning Map Amendment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The council held a public hearing on a request for annexation, utility extension, and UDO zoning map amendment from rural/commercial to Planned Development Residential (PDR 18.4) for 3815 Wake Forest Highway to allow up to 200 apartments and townhomes. Extensive public comment and council debate focused on traffic congestion, stormwater/floodplain impacts, school capacity, and affordable housing proffers.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed 4-3 (Annexation & UDO amendment passed 4-3; Consistency statement passed unanimously)

agenda_items.title: Public Hearing: MIS Durham Headquarters 2 Annexation and Zoning
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented a request for voluntary annexation and direct translational Industrial Light zoning for approximately 9.8 acres located at 3429 Industrial Drive to connect to city utilities. Following staff presentation and public input, the council approved the annexation and zoning items unanimously.

votes.item_title: Annexation and Utility Extension Agreement for 3815 Wake Forest Highway
votes.notes: Passed 4-3
votes.discussion_detail: The motion proposed adopting an ordinance to annex 3815 Wake Forest Highway into the city of Durham and authorizing the city manager to enter into a utility extension agreement with a Court Holdings LLC. During the preceding discussion, council members debated developer costs, community benefits, and broader housing market pressures, with extensive focus on negotiated profers. Key developer commitments finalized during the debate included increasing affordable units from 5% to 8%, raising the Durham Public Schools (DPS) profer to $43,000, mandating 100% native trees, and modifying green building requirements (retaining Duke Hero while removing Green Guard, Green Globe, and Energy Star). Ultimately, the annexation and utility extension agreement passed on a 4–3 vote. Council members Baker, Burrus, and Cook voted in opposition.

votes.item_title: UDO Zoning Map Amendment for 3815 Wake Forest Highway
votes.notes: Passed 4-3
votes.discussion_detail: The motion proposed adopting an ordinance amending the Unified Development Ordinance (UDO) to rezone the subject property at 3815 Wake Forest Highway from county jurisdiction (commercial neighborhood residential and residential suburban 20 within the Falls Jordan watershed overlay district B) to city jurisdiction as planned development residential 18.4 within the Falls Jordan watershed overlay district B. This zoning map amendment directly accompanied the annexation and utility extension agreement for the development site. Council debate leading into the vote covered the project's walkability, proximity to transit and commercial sites, and environmental considerations such as impervious surface limits set at 65%. The zoning map amendment passed by a 4–3 margin. Council members Baker, Burrus, and Cook dissented.

votes.item_title: Consistency Statement for 3815 Wake Forest Highway
votes.notes: Passed unanimously
votes.discussion_detail: The motion proposed adopting the required statutory consistency statement under North Carolina General Statute section 160D-6005 for the 3815 Wake Forest Highway development actions. Following the votes on annexation and rezoning, the consistency statement was moved, seconded, and passed unanimously. No council members voted in opposition.

meetings.title: Durham Joint City County Planning Committee (JCCPC) - September 2, 2026
meetings.executive_summary: Chair Nate Baker convened the September 2, 2026 JCCPC meeting, where the committee referred Item 8 (Neighborhood Meeting Guidelines) back to staff for additional engagement and unanimously approved the August 5 minutes. Staff presented Omnibus 20 (TC26003) aligning nine UDO articles with recent state legislation and clarifying textual versus graphic Traffic Impact Analysis (TIA) triggers, previewed three consolidated rezoning cases, and evaluated permit-processing barriers—earning unanimous informal consensus to reassess and eliminate the $11 annual street vendor registration fee. The meeting closed with an intense debate over the full draft Lakewood, West End, and Lyon Park Small Area Plan, as County Vice Chair Mike Lee warned that five-story redevelopment at Shops at Lakewood would accelerate property-tax displacement of longtime residents.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call, Agenda Adjustment (Item 8 Referred Back), and Approval of August 5 Minutes
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Chair Nate Baker called roll with Matt Kopac, Wendy Jacobs, and Stephen Valentine present at start, Shanetta Burris and Vice Chair Mike Lee joining shortly after, and Javiera Caballero joining during the meeting. The committee removed Item 8 (Neighborhood Meeting Guidelines) back to staff for further outreach and unanimously approved the August 5, 2026 minutes.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Approved minutes unanimously (voice vote); Item 8 referred back to staff

agenda_items.title: State Legislation Omnibus (TC26003 / Omnibus 20)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Robin Schultz and Planning Director Sara Young presented TC26003 updating nine UDO articles for state mandates—including direct Superior Court appeals, HB 372 Home-Based Business Fairness Act alignment, and Regulatory Reform Act glazing limits—while clarifying that graphic plans always trigger a TIA whereas textual plans trigger a TIA only above 150 peak-hour trips to avoid $60,000-$100,000 barriers for smaller projects. Kopac, Jacobs, Caballero, and Baker probed TIA timing, glazing pedestrian-level standards, max-buildout assumptions, and BPAC recommendations.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Case Preview (3 Cases)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff planner Javar Jones previewed three rezoning proposals inside the UGB requiring neither FGA exception nor TIA: 2123 Page Road (32.893 acres, PDR 10.105, up to 308 multifamily/townhouse units with 5% at 80% AMI for 30 years); Conover Road (1.13 acres, RR to RS-8 for 4-8 single-family homes); and 134 Robins Road (8.87 acres, RR to CG(D) textual for a hotel and event venue, on which Shanetta Burris flagged a public portal display bug).

agenda_items.title: Evaluation of Use Regulation Barriers During Permit Processing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Amber Egodan and Sara Young reviewed Comprehensive Plan Jobs & Training Actions 12 and 18 based on 90+ business contacts, peer benchmarking, FY26 permit metrics (2-3 day turnaround, 4.58/5 satisfaction), HB 372 updates, and the upcoming Clarity permitting portal (~18 months to go-live). Staff recommended eliminating the $11 annual street vendor registration fee, and JCCPC gave unanimous informal thumbs-up consensus for staff to proceed with fee-elimination analysis.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational with unanimous thumbs-up consensus to pursue eliminating $11 street vendor fee

agenda_items.title: Lakewood, West End, and Lyon Park Small Area Plan (Full Draft)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Sarah Long presented the five-chapter draft small area plan proposing up to five-story mixed-use (three-story transitions) and a 20% affordable housing target in the Shops at Lakewood TOA, micro-retail, expanded green space, paper-street trail connections (Norwood Ave, Dean/Gunter), cemetery GPR grants, Heritage Community designation, and <=3-story mixed-use along Chapel Hill Road. Vice Chair Mike Lee sharply criticized upzoning as worsening property-tax displacement, sparking broad debate with Caballero, Burris, Jacobs, Kopac, and Baker over balancing redevelopment with anti-displacement stabilization.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Informational / Scheduled for Oct 13 Planning Commission and Nov 5 Council work session

agenda_items.title: FY27 Community Planning Projects Tracker
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The committee received the informational monthly Community Planning Projects status tracker with no discussion before adjourning at 11:57 a.m.

votes.notes: Joint City-County Planning Committee voice vote; County Commissioners Wendy Jacobs, Stephen Valentine, and Vice Chair Mike Lee also participated, while Javiera Caballero joined later in the meeting.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham Joint City County Planning Committee (JCCPC) - September 2, 2026
disagreements.issue: Lakewood, West End, and Lyon Park Small Area Plan: Transit-Oriented Upzoning vs. Property-Tax Displacement
disagreements.summary: Committee members disagreed on whether the draft small area plan's five-story Transit Opportunity Area (TOA) redevelopment vision for Shops at Lakewood adequately protects legacy Black and low-income residents from rising property taxes and displacement.
disagreements.side_a_position: Warn that promoting large-scale redevelopment ahead of deep stabilization tools puts the plan 'backwards' and displaces longtime residents.
side_a_arguments: County Vice Chair Mike Lee argued forcefully that redeveloping Shops at Lakewood up to five stories will drive up surrounding assessments and property taxes, forcing remaining longtime residents out despite modest stabilization programs.
disagreements.side_b_position: Pursue mixed-use TOA density paired with 20% affordable housing goals, community land trust acquisitions, public-investment conditions, and CIP alignment.
side_b_arguments: Javiera Caballero, Shanetta Burris, Matt Kopac, Nate Baker, and County Commissioner Wendy Jacobs debated historical neighborhood shifts—noting West End retained greater Black and low-income stability via DCLT than Lyon Park's ~30% Black population drop.

Members argued targeted planning, tax relief, strings attached to any public investment in private sites like Scrap Exchange, and CIP alignment can create affordable units while avoiding passive stagnation.
disagreements.resolution: No formal JCCPC vote; staff forwarded the draft plan to the October 13 Planning Commission and November 5 City Council work session with committee feedback on anti-displacement.

agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff presentation on the development loan commitment of up to $6.3 million with Laurel Street Residential for 80 affordable rental units at 505 West Chapel Hill Street, preserving future development options for the remainder of the site.

agenda_items.title: City Strategic Plan Update and Discussion
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Comprehensive review and discussion of the city strategic plan, including the number of goals, naming conventions, inclusion of bikeability, carbon reduction climate resilience goals, and initiative descriptions.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session August 6, 2026
disagreements.issue: Proposed resolution supporting tenant union collective bargaining at Ashton and Willard Street apartments
disagreements.summary: Debate over whether the City Council should adopt a resolution supporting tenant union collective bargaining for seniors at Ashton and Willard Street apartments.
disagreements.side_a_position: Opposed consideration of the tenant resolution as an improper role for city government
side_a_arguments: Argued that a city resolution is not the proper tool to intervene in a private landlord-tenant dispute and that local government should not dictate negotiation tactics.
disagreements.side_b_position: Supported placing the resolution on the work session agenda
side_b_arguments: Argued that the council has a duty to support tenants, provide transparency, and discuss protections for seniors facing lease burdens and retaliation.
side_b_members: Council Member Baker, Council Member Cook, Council Member Kopack
disagreements.resolution: Agreed to place the resolution on a subsequent work session agenda to discuss both the resolution language and the proper role of local government.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session August 6, 2026
disagreements.issue: Requesting an early presentation from the Durham Housing Authority on HUD substantial default status
disagreements.summary: Debate on whether to require the Durham Housing Authority (DHA) to make an early presentation to the council regarding federal HUD substantial default status.
disagreements.side_a_position: Opposed early/special presentation request
side_a_arguments: Expressed concern that summoning DHA outside the scheduled annual update was viewed unfavorably as politically motivated criticism and that DHA staff were already hard at work responding to HUD.
disagreements.side_b_position: Supported scheduling an early informational presentation for transparency
side_b_arguments: Argued that public transparency and resident questions regarding HUD substantial default status necessitate an immediate informational presentation.
side_b_members: Council Member Cook, Council Member Baker
disagreements.resolution: No formal action taken; DHA to report back during its scheduled fall update.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting August 3, 2026
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council met on August 3, 2026, opening with ceremonial proclamations recognizing Haitians of the Triangle and Black Business Month ('Give It to the People'), followed by council member announcements on community events, state legislation (IOLTA funding, election bills), and unhoused population initiatives. The council held public hearings and approved three annexation and UDO amendment cases: Andrews Chapel Road townhouses (passed 5-2), Leesville Storage 2 (passed 4-3 after debate over self-storage land use on 30 acres), and 2106 Hensley Drive residential parcel (passed unanimously).

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, Ceremonial Proclamations, and Council Member Remarks
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Leonardo Williams called the meeting to order, followed by a moment of silence and the Pledge of Allegiance. Council members shared summer updates, discussed state and federal policy impacts (such as housing legislation, election bills, and the ending of the EBO program), and celebrated community achievements.

agenda_items.title: Setting Public Hearings and Consent Items
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The council set public hearings and handled routine administrative items, including confirmation of assessment rolls and setting upcoming public hearings.

agenda_items.title: Andrews Chapel Road Townhouses Annexation, UDO Amendment, and Consistency Statement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public hearing and consideration of the Andrews Chapel Road Townhouses annexation, utility extension agreement, PDR UDO amendment (28 townhomes), and consistency statement. Council discussed school student generation rates, stormwater/pond settling issues, and density. Passed 5-2 on annexation and UDO, and unanimously on consistency.

agenda_items.title: Leesville Storage 2 Annexation, UDO Amendment, and Consistency Statement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public hearing and consideration of the Leesville Storage 2 annexation, utility extension agreement, CGD UDO amendment (29.48 acres for self-storage), and consistency statement. Extensive debate regarding the 30-acre parcel size, compatibility with future corridor planning and highway commercial place type, and utility extension requirements for fire sprinklers. Passed 4-3 on annexation and UDO, and unanimously on consistency.

agenda_items.title: 2106 Hensley Drive Annexation, UDO Amendment, and Consistency Statement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public hearing and consideration of the 2106 Hensley Drive annexation, utility extension agreement, RS-20 UDO amendment, and consistency statement for a small 0.46-acre parcel requesting city water and sewer connection. Passed unanimously across all motions.

votes.item_title: Andrews Chapel Road Townhouses Annexation and Utility Extension Agreement
votes.notes: Passed 5-2
votes.discussion_detail: The city council considered an ordinance to annex the Andrews Chapel Road townhouses into the City of Durham and authorize a utility extension agreement with Nareda G. Balajanda. Council members discussed home investments, building permits, compact testing, and engineering/professional licenses as checks and balances in the building science profession. The motion passed by a 5-2 vote, with Council Members Baker and Burris voting in the negative. Dissenting members opposed the proposal amid general caution regarding quality assurance, structural durability, and potential homeowner investment risks.

votes.item_title: Andrews Chapel Road UDO Amendment (Planned Development Residential 6.085)
votes.notes: Passed 5-2
votes.discussion_detail: The city council considered an ordinance amending the unified development ordinance to take the Andrews Chapel Road property out of county residential jurisdiction and establish it as Planned Development Residential 6.085 within city jurisdiction. Discussion centered around the project's adherence to standards, tree replacement, impervious surface limits, and dedicated housing fund contributions. The motion passed 5-2, with Council Members Baker and Burris voting no. The dissent reflects ongoing council scrutiny regarding new residential developments and zoning changes.

votes.item_title: Andrews Chapel Road Consistency Statement (NCGS 160D-605)
votes.notes: Passed unanimously
votes.discussion_detail: The city council considered a motion to adopt the consistency statement required by North Carolina General Statute Section 160D-605 for the Andrews Chapel Road project. Following brief procedural remarks where council members noted jumping the gun on voting, the motion was opened and passed unanimously.

votes.item_title: Leesville Storage 2 Annexation and Utility Extension Agreement
votes.notes: Passed 4-3
votes.discussion_detail: The city council evaluated a request from Andy Porter of TLA Associates for a voluntary annexation and utility extension agreement for three parcels totaling 29.48 acres located at 2935 US 70 Highway East, 4615, and 4627 Leesville Road (Leesville Storage 2). Discussion addressed site layout details, power line restrictions by Duke Power prohibiting use under lines due to fire safety liabilities, and the inclusion of a parcel across the power lines. After a revote due to a card recording issue, the annexation and utility agreement passed 4-3, with Mayor Pro Tem Caballero, Council Member Baker, and Council Member Cook voting no over concerns regarding land utility and project boundaries.

votes.item_title: Leesville Storage 2 UDO Amendment (Commercial General & CGD)
votes.notes: Passed 4-3
votes.discussion_detail: The city council evaluated a companion UDO amendment for Leesville Storage 2 to establish commercial general and commercial general with a textual development plan (Falls Jordan District B Watershed Protection Overlay) under city jurisdiction. Staff presented details on the 29.48-acre request and place type consistency. Following the annexation vote, the UDO amendment passed 4-3, with Mayor Pro Tem Caballero and Council Members Baker and Cook voting in opposition.

votes.item_title: Leesville Storage 2 Consistency Statement (NCGS 160D-605)
votes.notes: Passed unanimously
votes.discussion_detail: This vote concerned the adoption of a consistency statement under North Carolina General Statute Section 160D-605 for the Leesville Storage 2 project. The discussion leading up to the votes on this matter touched on complex issues regarding parcel annexations, power line constraints by Duke Power, and parcel adjustments. The consistency statement motion passed unanimously following prior votes on the project's annexation and UDO amendments.

votes.item_title: 2106 Hensley Drive Annexation and Utility Extension Agreement
votes.notes: Passed unanimously
votes.discussion_detail: This vote involved a request for a utility extension agreement, voluntary annexation, and initial zoning map change for a .46-acre parcel located at 2106 Hinesley Drive, submitted by individual landowner Jeffrey De La Rosa Garcia to build a family home. During the public hearing, the applicant briefly explained that the project is straightforward and solely intended for family residential use. The council closed the public hearing without further questions and unanimously approved the annexation and utility extension agreement ordinance.

votes.item_title: 2106 Hensley Drive UDO Amendment (Residential Suburban 20)
votes.notes: Passed unanimously
votes.discussion_detail: This vote concerned an ordinance amending the unified development ordinance by taking the 2106 Hinesley Drive property out of residential suburban 20 county jurisdiction and establishing it under residential suburban 20 city jurisdiction. The applicant, Jeffrey De La Rosa Garcia, explained during the public hearing that the request supports building a home for his family. Following the public hearing, the council approved the UDO amendment ordinance unanimously.

votes.item_title: 2106 Hensley Drive Consistency Statement (NCGS 160D-605)
votes.notes: Passed unanimously
votes.discussion_detail: This vote involved the adoption of the required consistency statement under North Carolina General Statute Section 160D-605 for the 2106 Hinesley Drive annexation and UDO amendment. Following unanimous approval of the related annexation and UDO amendment ordinances for the residential property, the consistency statement motion was also approved unanimously.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting August 3, 2026
disagreements.issue: Leesville Storage 2 Annexation and UDO Amendment (30 acres for self-storage)
disagreements.summary: Discussion on whether dedicating 30 acres of highway commercial land to self-storage aligns with long-term corridor vision and urban connectivity goals.
disagreements.side_a_position: Support annexation and commercial zoning for self-storage project
side_a_arguments: Project is consistent with 22 of 24 comprehensive plan policies and highway commercial place type.
Steep topography and Duke Power transmission easements limit alternative development potential.
Applicant is dedicating right-of-way for turn lanes on Leesville Road/US 70 and keeping impervious surface low (~21%).
Planning Commission recommended unanimous approval.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose 30-acre self-storage annexation due to land use and future corridor vision concerns
side_b_arguments: 30 acres of prime commercial highway corridor land should be reserved for more integrated, walkable, or higher-efficiency urban uses rather than self-storage.
Concerns regarding future boulevarding and corridor vision for US 70.
disagreements.resolution: Passed 4-3, with Mayor Pro Tem Caballero and Council Members Baker and Cook voting no.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting August 3, 2026
disagreements.issue: Andrews Chapel Road Townhouses Annexation and PDR UDO Amendment
disagreements.summary: Debate over housing density versus suburban sprawl and auto-centric development patterns.
disagreements.side_a_position: Support townhouse development and density
side_a_arguments: Aligns with the comprehensive plan (91% policy alignment), adds needed housing density and connectivity.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose sprawl and auto-centric development
side_b_arguments: Concerns over auto-centric development and sprawl.
disagreements.resolution: Passed 5-2, with Council Members Baker and Burris voting no.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session August 3, 2026
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council held its post-July recess work session on August 3, 2026, presided over by Mayor Williams. Key discussions centered on public comments regarding unhoused encampments, neighborhood concerns over noise and traffic violations from the new El Toro Loco swap meet/flea market, and staff updates on the Racial Equity Commission, the 2026 Appropriations Act and Equal Business Opportunity Program (EBOP) repeal, project management consulting services, street closures for public events, protected bike lane contracts, and lift station maintenance. The council also approved an excused absence for Council Member Burris for an upcoming work session and settled the agenda.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order & Opening Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Williams called the work session to order after the July recess, followed by roll call and council member announcements, including the introduction of summer intern Mikayla Rust and new fellow Hannah Sebastian from the Bloomberg Harvard Mayor's Program.

agenda_items.title: Project Management Consulting Services Amendment (Pulled Item 7)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council discussed the fourth amendment to the project management consulting services agreement with Turner & Townsend Heery LLC, reviewing project volume increases, fee structures, and staffing augmentation models.

agenda_items.title: Street Closures for Open Streets & Holiday Parade (Pulled Item 8)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed street closures for the 2026 Movable City Open Streets and Holiday Parade, discussing potential shifts of the parade to an evening schedule and coordination with the downtown tree lighting.

agenda_items.title: Public Comment: Unhoused Encampments & Housing Funds
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public speakers raised urgent concerns regarding unhoused encampments at Oakwood Park and Fayetteville Street, citing the need for sustainable transitional housing and better support services. Council members and the city manager discussed ongoing efforts around the homelessness strategic plan.

agenda_items.title: Bike Lane Vertical Protection & Neighborhood Bike Routes (Pulled Item 11)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation staff presented the construction contract for bike lane vertical protection and neighborhood bike routes on Main Street and MLK Jr. Parkway, and public speaker David Bradway spoke in support of expanding protected cycling infrastructure.

agenda_items.title: Lift Station Improvements Contract Amendment (Pulled Item 14)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed amendment three to the professional engineering services contract with Highfill Infrastructure Engineering PC for FY21 lift station improvements, confirming focus on public lift stations.

agenda_items.title: Public Comment: El Toro Loco Swap Meet & Noise Complaints
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Nearby residents and community members spoke out against the grand opening and unpermitted operations of the El Toro Loco swap meet and flea market, highlighting severe noise ordinance violations, traffic congestion, and safety concerns.

agenda_items.title: Racial Equity Commission Appointment (Pulled Item 2)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Former youth representative Efio Tijagun spoke during the discussion of pulled Item 2 regarding her resignation from the Racial Equity Commission, citing communication breakdowns and turnover within the Community Partnerships and Engagement office.

agenda_items.title: 2026 Appropriations Act & EBOP Ordinance Repeal (Pulled Item 6)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Deputy CFO Sheila Faucette presented on the impact of the state 2026 Appropriations Act (Session Law 2026-41) repealing the Equal Business Opportunity Program ordinance, and council discussed strategies using small local business programs and federal funding rules.

votes.item_title: Excused absence for Council Member Burris
votes.discussion_detail: Council Member Burris requested an excused absence from Thursday's work session due to travel. The motion was moved, seconded, and approved unanimously by a 6-0 vote.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting June 15, 2026
meetings.executive_summary: During the June 15, 2026 Durham City Council meeting, the council reviewed proclamations, heard public comments, and addressed significant agenda items including the FY 2026-2027 budget, a 12-month data center and cryptocurrency mining moratorium extension, housing code updates, and several major zoning/land use decisions. The council approved the Garland District rezoning in East Durham (5-2) and the Palmer Edge tier change and rezoning for manufacturing economic development, alongside unanimous passage of the data center moratorium extension. The meeting concluded with council comments before adjourning for summer break until August.

agenda_items.title: Opening & Roll Call
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Meeting called to order by Mayor Leonardo Williams. Opening moment of silence and Pledge of Allegiance led by Council Member Rist. Roll call confirmed all council members present.

agenda_items.title: Announcements by Council
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council members shared recent community updates, acknowledged community losses including Minister Paul Scott and Thomas Crowalbriden, discussed the 2026 Stanley Cup victory by the Carolina Hurricanes, and noted local events for Juneteenth and Pride Month.

agenda_items.title: Ceremonial Items & Proclamations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council presented proclamations recognizing July 2026 as Cleft and Craniofacial Awareness Month (featuring Ada Prikopac and the Duke Cleft/Craniofacial team), honoring Lela Cash Coley-Royster on her 95th birthday, and proclaiming Tourette Syndrome Awareness Day (featuring Scarlett Romana).

agenda_items.item_number: City Manager's Report & Water Restrictions Briefing
agenda_items.title: City Manager's Report & Water Restrictions Briefing
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Bo Ferguson introduced priority items, and Water Management Director Don Greeley provided an overview of the severe drought conditions prompting the transition to stage two water restrictions effective today.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The consent agenda containing routine administrative, advisory, and contractual items was presented. Items 12, 14, 15, 17, and 38 were pulled for separate discussion and voting.

agenda_items.title: FY 2026-27 Budget Adoption
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Extensive deliberation and public comment on the fiscal year 2026-2027 budget and capital improvement plan. Council members discussed the challenges of balancing the budget amidst revenue shortfalls, property tax valuation appeals, minimum living wage increases, and funding for community nonprofits and housing.

agenda_items.title: Public Comments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public comments on general topics including crime reporting, law enforcement support, and community activism.

agenda_items.title: Citizens Advisory Committee Appointments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Appointments made to the Citizens Advisory Committee, Durham Workers' Rights Commission, and other boards.

agenda_items.item_number: Item 16 / City Council Meeting Schedule Revision
agenda_items.title: City Council Meeting Schedule Revision
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Discussion and vote on revising the 2026 city council meeting schedule (option to reschedule September meeting).

agenda_items.item_number: Items 7, 8, 9 / Garland District Rezoning & Utility Agreement
agenda_items.title: Garland District Rezoning & Utility Agreement
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public hearing and deliberation on the Garland District consolidated zoning map change (Industrial Light to Commercial General & Commercial Infill) and utility extension agreement with Garland Ventures LLC.

agenda_items.item_number: Items 10, 11 / Development Moratoria UDO Text Amendment
agenda_items.title: Development Moratoria UDO Text Amendment
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public hearing and adoption of Unified Development Ordinance text amendment (TC2600002) removing barriers and redundant standards for instituting development moratoria.

agenda_items.item_number: Item 12 / Data Centers & Crypto Mining Moratorium Extension
agenda_items.title: Data Centers & Crypto Mining Moratorium Extension
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public hearing and adoption of a 10-month extension (12-month total) of the temporary moratorium on development approvals for data centers, cryptocurrency mining, and related high-impact data processing facilities.

agenda_items.item_number: Items 13, 14, 15 / Palmer Edge Development Tier & Rezoning
agenda_items.title: Palmer Edge Development Tier & Rezoning
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public hearings and deliberations on the Palmer Edge Light Industrial Park development tier change (Urban to Suburban) and Z2600002 rezoning with textual development plan.

agenda_items.title: Minimum Housing Code Amendments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public hearing and presentation on proposed amendments to the Minimum Housing Code (Chapter 10, Article 6) to modernize standards and improve resident health and safety.

votes.item_title: Civilian Police Review Board Appointments (James Lehman, Arnold Eatmon, Carol Devera Johnson, Catherine Sullivan)
votes.discussion_detail: Returning to pulled item 15 from the consent agenda following a recess, the council addressed appointments to the Civilian Police Review Board. A motion was offered to confirm the city manager's appointment of James Lehman, Arnold Eatmon, Carol Devera Johnson, and Catherine Sullivan to the board. The terms for these newly confirmed members were established to expire on June 30, 2030. The motion was moved and properly seconded, and upon opening and closing the vote by the Madam Clerk, the appointments were approved unanimously by a 7-0 vote.

votes.item_title: Civilian Police Review Board Reappointment (Kendra Presley)
votes.discussion_detail: Continuing with the pulled Civilian Police Review Board items following item 15, the council considered the reappointment of Kendra Presley. A motion was entertained to confirm the city manager's reappointment of Presley to the board. The term for this reappointment was similarly set to expire on June 30, 2030. Following a proper motion and second, the clerk opened the vote, and the motion passed unanimously with a 7-0 vote.

votes.item_title: Contract for Landlord Engagement Services with HOM Incorporated
votes.discussion_detail: The council took up pulled item 17, concerning a contract for landlord engagement services with HOM Incorporated. A motion was presented to authorize the city manager to execute the contract with HOM Incorporated to provide landlord engagement services in an amount not to exceed $400,000. After being moved and properly seconded, the vote was opened by the clerk amidst brief administrative clarifications regarding public comment duplicate entries. The motion passed unanimously with a 7-0 vote.

votes.item_title: 2026 First Quarter Crime Report
votes.discussion_detail: The council evaluated item 38, the 2026 first quarter crime report, which had been pulled during the consent agenda. Public commenter Ms. Peterson addressed the council, expressing strong concern over disrespect shown to law enforcement officers during the meeting, detailing community crime issues, her own recent vehicle break-in, and advocating for increased police pay and the restoration of a neighborhood satellite police station on Ridgeway Avenue. Following public comments, a motion was made and seconded to receive the 2026 first quarter crime report. The clerk opened the vote, and the motion passed unanimously by a 7-0 vote.

votes.item_title: Citizens Advisory Committee Appointments (Lily Burdick, David J. McColl, Kayla Rudisill)
votes.discussion_detail: The council addressed item 35 regarding Citizens Advisory Committee appointments for Lily Burdick, David J. McColl, and Kayla Rudisill. The Madam Clerk presented the nominees to fill vacancies on the Citizens Advisory Committee with terms expiring on June 30th, 2027 and June 30th, 2029. Following the motion and second, the vote was opened and closed, passing unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Garland District Utility Extension Agreement with Garland Ventures LLC
votes.discussion_detail: The council considered a utility extension agreement with Garland Ventures LLC. Concerns were raised regarding whether approving the agreement and rezoning bypassed a more holistic small area planning opportunity or design studio charrette, as well as potential lack of anti-displacement and environmental sustainability protections without proffers. Council Member Cook voiced opposition because she did not want to set a standard for approving developments without binding protections, while supporters noted active engagement from neighborhood residents and business owners. Ultimately, the motion to authorize the utility extension agreement passed 5-2, with Council Members Baker and Cook voting nay.

votes.item_title: Garland District Zoning Map Change (Industrial Light to Commercial General & Commercial Infill)
votes.discussion_detail: The council considered a zoning map change for the Garland District, taking property out of Industrial Light (IL) and establishing the same as Commercial General (CG) and Commercial Infill (CI). Discussion centered around small area planning, community investment, and whether the zoning transition should include formal proffers or anti-displacement commitments. Council Members Baker and Cook opposed the change due to concerns about the lack of binding environmental and anti-displacement protections in the current zoning structure. Despite these concerns, the motion to adopt the zoning ordinance passed 5-2, with Baker and Cook voting nay.

votes.item_title: Garland District Consistency Statement (NCGS 160D-605)
votes.discussion_detail: The council considered adopting a consistency statement as required by North Carolina General Statute Section 160D-605 regarding the Garland District rezoning. Following the previous motions on the utility extension and zoning map change, the motion was duly moved and seconded. The clerk opened and closed the vote, which passed unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Development Moratoria UDO Text Amendment (TC2600002)
votes.discussion_detail: The council considered a staff-initiated text amendment (TC2600002) to the Unified Development Ordinance regarding development moratoria. Robin Schultz from the Planning and Development Department presented that the amendment removes additional barriers imposed by the UDO on governing bodies instituting a development moratorium and eliminates redundant standards already required by NC General Statute Section 160D-107. Staff noted that this text amendment was necessary in order to approve the subsequent proposed moratorium extension on data centers. Following the public hearing where no speakers signed up, the council voted unanimously 7-0 to adopt the ordinance incorporating revisions to Article 3, Applications and Permits.

votes.item_title: Development Moratoria Consistency Statement (NCGS 160D-605)
votes.discussion_detail: Robin Schultz from the Planning and Development Department presented a staff-initiated text amendment (TC2600002) to remove UDO barriers and redundant state standards for instituting development moratoria. Following a closed public hearing with no registered speakers, the council unanimously approved the text amendment ordinance. Subsequently, the council adopted the required North Carolina General Statute Section 160D-605 consistency statement by a 7-0 vote.

votes.item_title: Data Centers & Cryptocurrency Mining Moratorium Extension (10-Month Extension / 12-Month Total)
votes.discussion_detail: Sarah Young with the Planning and Development Department presented a proposed 10-month extension—totaling 12 months—of the temporary moratorium on development approvals for data centers, cryptocurrency mining operations, and associated data processing facilities under NCGS 160D-107. Council members discussed specific expansion language covering existing data centers, necessary carve-outs for hospital facilities, and insights from community groups like Toxic-Free NC and attorneys Reberg and Miles. The discussion also touched upon regional coordination through the JCCPC, local RTP partners, and the massive energy demands associated with AI and data infrastructure. With minor language clarifications read into the record by staff regarding expansions and carve-outs, the council voted unanimously to adopt the ordinance.

votes.item_title: Palmer Edge Light Industrial Park Development Tier Change (Urban to Suburban)
votes.discussion_detail: Attorney Patrick Byker presented a request on behalf of Parmer Edge and AbbVie Inc. to change the development tier from urban to suburban for approximately 185 to 190 acres to facilitate an RTP-like campus design with increased green space and pervious surfaces. During discussions, Council Member Rist and Mayor Pro Tem Caballero raised concerns regarding land-use efficiency and proximity to existing transit routes and future BRT corridors along 147 and 85. While supporting the economic development opportunity, Council Member Rist voted against the tier change, arguing that suburban-style development is an inefficient use of land near transit infrastructure. The resolution amending the tier boundary ultimately passed with a 6-1 vote, with Council Member Rist casting the lone dissenting vote.

votes.item_title: Palmer Edge 2 Zoning Map Change (Industrial Light with Textual Development Plan)
votes.discussion_detail: Peyton Burgess of the Planning and Development Department presented a zoning map change request submitted by Elliott Brewer with Carlin Real Estate for seven parcels totaling 57.17 acres along Glover and Rigsby roads, proposing to rezone them from residential, rural, and industrial light to industrial light with a textual development plan. Attorney Patrick Byker explained that the project, designated Parmer Edge 2, relates to previous annexations and may incorporate a much-needed Duke Power substation to provide utility redundancy for downtown and East Durham. Council members questioned applicant representatives regarding comprehensive plan consistency, native plant landscaping commitments, and site engineering uncertainties. Following clarifications from the applicant regarding nursery inventory constraints and site constraints, the council voted unanimously to adopt the ordinance amending the UDO and zoning designation.

votes.item_title: Palmer Edge 2 Consistency Statement (NCGS 160D-605)
votes.discussion_detail: Following the approval of the Palmer Edge 2 zoning map change, the mayor presented the required North Carolina General Statute Section 160D-605 consistency statement for adoption. The motion was properly moved and seconded. The council voted unanimously (7-0) to approve the consistency statement.

votes.item_title: Minimum Housing Code Amendments (Chapter 10, Article 6)
votes.discussion_detail: Alexis John, Assistant Director of Housing and Neighborhood Services, presented proposed modifications to the city's minimum housing code, marking its first major update since 2016. The department reviewed standards across multiple North Carolina municipalities and collaborated with the National Center for Healthy Housing to align Durham's code with national standards and the International Property Maintenance Code. The amendments focus on improving resident health and safety, clarifying requirements, increasing enforcement consistency, and modernizing the code. Following the public hearing where no speakers registered, the council unanimously adopted the ordinance amending Chapter 10, Article 6 of the City of Durham Code of Ordinances in a 7-0 vote.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting June 15, 2026
disagreements.issue: Garland District Rezoning (Commercial General/Infill vs Industrial Light)
disagreements.summary: Debate over whether to rezone the Garland District from light industrial to commercial general/infill to encourage mixed-use and small business revival versus concerns over lack of developer proffers and community protections.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve rezoning to Commercial General and Commercial Infill.
side_a_arguments: Current light industrial zoning allows heavy nuisances/junkyards and is inappropriate for the neighborhood; rezoning supports local small business revitalization and foot traffic in East Durham.
disagreements.side_b_position: Vote against the rezoning.
side_b_arguments: Lack of robust community protections, anti-displacement measures, or proffers for infrastructure/schools; concerns over commercial development dynamics without adequate developer contributions.
disagreements.resolution: Passed 5-2 (Council Members Baker and Cook voted no).

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Meeting June 15, 2026
disagreements.issue: Palmer Edge Development Tier Change (Urban to Suburban Tier)
disagreements.summary: Discussion on modifying the development tier from urban to suburban for the Palmer Edge Light Industrial Park to support major manufacturing investments versus transit-oriented land efficiency concerns.
disagreements.side_a_position: Support the tier change to suburban to foster economic development.
side_a_arguments: Necessary to accommodate a state-of-the-art manufacturing facility (AbbVie) requiring a campus environment with green space, trees, and setbacks.
disagreements.side_b_position: Vote against the suburban tier change.
side_b_arguments: Suburban-style low density land use is inefficient and less ideal near transit corridors compared to dense urban planning.
disagreements.resolution: Passed 6-1 (Council Member Rist voted no).

meetings.title: Adoption of the Fiscal Year 2026-27 Budget on June 15, 2026
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council met on June 15, 2026, to consider the adoption of the Fiscal Year 2026-27 budget, the Fiscal Year 2027-32 Capital Improvement Plan (CIP), and related ordinances. After hearing public comments regarding nonprofit funding, immigrant legal defense services, housing, taxes, and public safety, the council discussed the complex and challenging nature of the budget process. Ultimately, the council voted unanimously to adopt the budget, CIP, and related ordinances as printed in the published agenda.

agenda_items.title: Fiscal Year 2026-27 Budget and FY 2027-32 CIP Adoption
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Council opened the public hearing and deliberated on the Fiscal Year 2026-27 Budget and FY 2027-32 Capital Improvement Plan (CIP). Public commenters raised concerns regarding nonprofit funding, immigrant legal defense, housing needs, and property tax assessments, while council members discussed the challenges of balancing an austere general fund budget without a property tax increase.

votes.item_title: Fiscal Year 2026-27 Budget and FY 2027-32 CIP Adoption
votes.discussion_detail: The Durham City Council considered and adopted the Fiscal Year 2026-27 budget, FY 2027-32 capital improvement plan (CIP) ordinance, and related ordinances as presented in the published agenda. Prior to the vote, public commenters addressed the council regarding budget concerns and tax impacts, prompting clarifications on city versus county tax roles. Following discussion, a motion was made and seconded to approve the budget package as printed. The council voted unanimously (7-0) to pass the motion, with members noting the exceptional difficulty of crafting this year's budget and acknowledging the diverse perspectives represented in the final consensus.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Work Session June 4, 2026
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council held a work session on June 4, 2026, discussing major items including an expiring letter of credit for the Durham City Transit Company, the 2026 meeting schedule adjustment, an eviction diversion program contract update, the Q1 crime report, and the disparity study final report. The council formally voted to approve letter of credit authorizations for the transit company after suspending the rules, agreed to hold a closed session, and settled the upcoming meeting agenda.

agenda_items.title: Roll Call & Opening Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Williams and Council members convened the work session, followed by the City Clerk calling the roll. Council members and the city manager shared brief announcements regarding community events, budget deliberations, and upcoming groundmakings.

agenda_items.title: Priority Items and Closed Session Authorization
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Manager and City Attorney presented priority items for the agenda, including withdrawals and items to be pulled or suspended. The City Attorney requested a closed session regarding threatened liability claims.

agenda_items.title: Summer Legal Intern Introductions & Board Nominations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council introduced three summer legal interns working with the city attorney's office and discussed upcoming board/commission nominations.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Reading and Item Pulls
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council reviewed and read through the consent agenda items, pulling several items for separate discussion and voting.

agenda_items.title: DCTC Letter of Credit & Rule Suspension
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Finance staff presented the letter of credit requirements for the Durham City Transit Company (DCTC) assurance program. Council suspended rules and voted to authorize the application and agreements with JPM Chase and Travelers Indemnity Company.

agenda_items.title: Public Comment Session
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Public speakers addressed the council on various topics including property tax equity for multifamily housing trash collection and community memory in municipal governance.

agenda_items.title: Revision to 2026 City Council Meeting Schedule
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council discussed proposed revisions to the 2026 City Council meeting schedule, specifically addressing conflicts with religious holidays such as Yom Kippur and evaluating alternative meeting dates.

agenda_items.title: Eviction Diversion Program Contract Amendment (Legal Aid of NC)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council engaged in extensive debate regarding the first amendment to the contract for administration of the Eviction Diversion Program with Legal Aid of North Carolina, discussing funding balances, tenant rights, mediation, and coordination with county rental assistance.
agenda_items.vote_summary: Passed later or discussed extensively (Disagreement noted)

agenda_items.title: Police Department 2026 First Quarter Crime Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Police Chief Tate and staff presented the 2026 first quarter crime report, covering violent crime statistics, clearance rates, recruitment numbers, gun thefts from vehicles, and domestic violence.

agenda_items.title: 2025 City of Durham Disparity Study Final Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Dave Miller of Miller Consulting presented the final report of the 2025 City of Durham Disparity Study, highlighting utilization disparities across procurement categories and recommending steps from awareness to action.

votes.item_title: Closed Session Authorization
votes.notes: Pursuant to NC General Statute 143-318.11A3
votes.discussion_detail: The City Attorney requested and moved to hold a closed session pursuant to North Carolina General Statute 143-318.11A3 for attorney-client consultation regarding a threatened but not yet filed liability claim. The motion was seconded and approved unanimously by voice vote at the conclusion of the meeting.

votes.item_title: Suspend Rules for Item 21 (Letter of Credit)
votes.notes: To allow immediate vote during work session
votes.discussion_detail: A procedural motion was introduced to suspend the rules in order to consider and vote on agenda item number 21 regarding a letter of credit for the Durham City Transit Company Assurance Program. The motion received a proper second and was passed unanimously by a voice vote.

votes.item_title: Authorize Letter of Credit Application from JPM Chase (Not to exceed $450,000)
votes.notes: Item 21
votes.discussion_detail: The council considered agenda item number 21 to authorize the city manager or his designee to apply for a letter of credit from JPMorgan Chase and Company in an amount not to exceed $450,000. Staff explained that the letter of credit is required as collateral by Travelers Indemnity Company for open historical liability claims from 2022-2023 when DCTC managed GoDurham under a high-deductible policy. Following questions regarding why a letter of credit is required for DCTC unlike the city's self-insured retention plan, the motion passed unanimously by a voice vote.

votes.item_title: Authorize Letter of Credit Agreement to Travelers Indemnity Company
votes.notes: Item 21
votes.discussion_detail: Following the letter of credit application authorization, a motion was presented to authorize the city manager or designee to issue the letter of credit agreement to Travelers Indemnity Company. Staff noted that the underlying policy is an incurred space policy remaining open for claims up through the statute of limitations expiring at the end of the month. The motion was properly seconded and carried unanimously via voice vote.

votes.item_title: Authorize Execution of Legal Documents for Travelers Indemnity Letter of Credit Requirements
votes.notes: Item 21
votes.discussion_detail: The council considered the final component of agenda item number 21, moving to authorize the city manager or designee to execute any applications, renewals, amendments, and associated legal documents necessary to meet Travelers Indemnity Company's letter of credit requirements. The motion included authorization to make pre-execution changes to legal documents provided they remain consistent with the intent of the agenda item memo. The motion was seconded and approved unanimously by voice vote.

disagreements.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session June 4, 2026
disagreements.issue: Eviction Diversion Program Contract & Funding Balance
disagreements.summary: Discussion over the contract extension for Legal Aid of North Carolina's Eviction Diversion Program sparked a policy debate regarding whether municipal funds are disproportionately allocated to legal services versus direct rental assistance.
disagreements.side_a_position: Skeptical of heavy investment in legal aid without commensurate direct rental assistance and comprehensive root-cause analysis.
side_a_arguments: Expressed concern that funding is lopsided toward legal defense rather than direct financial rental assistance, questioned program efficiency, and emphasized addressing root causes of housing instability.
disagreements.side_b_position: Strongly supported legal aid and mediation as vital stabilizing protections for tenants facing swift evictions under state law.
side_b_arguments: Argued that legal representation, tenant advocacy, and mediation are crucial due to North Carolina's heavily landlord-favorable laws and the severe eviction crisis.
disagreements.resolution: No formal split vote was taken during the work session; the contract discussion concluded with agreement to evaluate broader housing and rental assistance coordination through ongoing planning and joint city-county discussions.
